activityLevelNote: Use these descriptions to determine which column applies to tasks performed in your workplace. Many jobs involve more than one activity level during a shift — use the highest level sustained for 30 minutes or more as the basis for work-rest decisions. Metabolic rate ranges are based on NIOSH workload categories; for more precise estimation by task, consult ISO 8996:2021 (Ergonomics of the thermal environment — Determination of metabolic rate) or the 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities (Herrmann et al., 2024).

confirmedVsUnconfirmed.heading: ⚠ What is confirmed vs. what still requires direct curve reading.
confirmed: The Recommended Alert Limit (RAL, for unacclimatized workers) and Recommended Exposure Limit (REL, for acclimatized workers) equations for 60 min/h (continuous work): RAL = 59.9 − 14.1 log₁₀(M[W]); REL = 56.7 − 11.5 log₁₀(M[W])
Continuous-work REL thresholds: Light ≈ 30°C (Table 5-1); Moderate ≈ 28°C (Table 5-1); Heavy = 26°C (equation + Table 5-1); Very Heavy ≈ 25°C (Table 5-1)
Continuous-work RAL thresholds: Light ≈ 26.5°C (equation); Moderate ≈ 25°C (NIOSH text, p. 4); Heavy ≈ 22.3°C (equation); Very Heavy ≈ 20.9°C (equation)
RAL/REL framework, four-line structure (15/30/45/60 min/h), clothing assumption, standard man, and acclimatization protocols — all confirmed NIOSH (2016)
confirmedVsUnconfirmed.requiresDirectReading: All 45/15, 30/30, and 15/45 WBGT thresholds — the figures present these as graphical curves only; no equations are given for the non-continuous work-rest lines. Cells marked * in the WBGT tab are approximate and should be verified against the figures before use in enforcement or published tools.
derivedApproximations: T+RH tab unacclimatized thresholds — derived by shifting acclimatized HI breakpoints; no equivalent NIOSH published table in HI units
Heat Index tab unacclimatized table — similarly derived; NIOSH Recommended Alert Limits (RAL) is expressed in WBGT, not HI

hiMethodology.heading: Methodology for Heat Index–Based Work-Rest Limits
hiMethodology.body: NIOSH expresses both the Recommended Exposure Limit (REL, for acclimatized workers) and the Recommended Alert Limit (RAL, for unacclimatized workers) in Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) units — not Heat Index. The Temperature + Humidity and Heat Index tabs in this tool use Heat Index as a practical field substitute because it requires no specialized instrumentation and is accessible to workers and supervisors without industrial hygiene training.
hiMethodology.acclimatizedNote: Heat Index thresholds were established using OSHA's published Heat Index risk framework as the structural basis (Lower Risk / Moderate / High / Very High / Extreme), which maps onto the NIOSH REL risk continuum. Work-rest cycles at each Heat Index level were assigned by cross-referencing the approximate WBGT equivalent for a given Heat Index value against the NIOSH (2016) REL curves (Figures 8-1 and 8-2). The approximate WBGT-to-Heat Index relationship used is: at moderate humidity (~50% RH), WBGT ≈ 0.70 × Wet Bulb Temperature + 0.30 × Dry Bulb Temperature; and Heat Index ≈ Dry Bulb Temperature + a humidity adjustment. This yields a rough correspondence of approximately 1–2°C WBGT per 5°F Heat Index under moderate indoor conditions, though this relationship varies significantly with relative humidity and air movement.
hiMethodology.unacclimatizedNote: No NIOSH-published table expresses the Recommended Alert Limit (RAL) in Heat Index units. The unacclimatized thresholds in this tool are approximated by shifting the acclimatized (REL-based) Heat Index breakpoints downward by approximately 8–10°F (4–5°C equivalent). This offset is derived from the difference between the NIOSH REL and RAL continuous-work equations at representative metabolic rates — for example, at moderate work (300 kcal/h), the REL continuous-work threshold is ≈27.5°C WBGT and the RAL is ≈24.0°C WBGT, a difference of approximately 3.5°C. Accounting for the approximate WBGT-to-HI conversion, this translates to roughly 8–10°F lower Heat Index thresholds for unacclimatized workers. These are approximations only and have not been validated against a published NIOSH source.
hiMethodology.limitations: Heat Index was developed for shade conditions with light air movement (~5 mph). It does not account for: (1) radiant heat from hot equipment, ovens, or surfaces — a major factor in kitchens, laundries, and foundries; (2) very low or very high air velocity; (3) PPE or impermeable clothing; or (4) individual metabolic rate. In any environment with significant radiant heat sources or unusual clothing, WBGT measurement is strongly preferred and the Heat Index tab values should not be relied upon for compliance or enforcement purposes.

methodologyNotes.nioshCeilingNote: ⚠ The 2016 NIOSH update removed the 1986 ceiling limits. The 1986 criteria included absolute ceiling WBGT values above which no work was recommended. NIOSH (2016) explicitly removed these: "Data and scientific evidence were not identified to continue to support the NIOSH ceiling limit recommendations. Acclimatized workers live and work in temperatures above the ceiling limit without adverse health effects." The DANGER! designation in this tool therefore does not reflect a NIOSH-defined ceiling; it indicates conditions where the work-rest curves cannot provide protection using work-practice controls alone and where engineering controls, physiological monitoring, or cessation of work should be evaluated by a qualified safety professional.
indoorConsiderations: Tables assume indoor setting with no direct solar load. All WBGT values assume natural WBGT (NWBGTi) or indoor measurement.

Radiant heat sources (ovens, machinery, steam lines, dryers) can dramatically elevate effective heat stress beyond what air temperature or heat index captures. WBGT measured on-site is the only reliable method in these environments.
Air movement matters: fans can reduce heat stress significantly; still air in a hot room is more hazardous than the dry-bulb temperature alone suggests.
PPE and clothing dramatically affect allowable exposure. Impermeable suits can require reducing thresholds by 10–11°C WBGT equivalent.

standardsComparison.name: NIOSH REL/RAL (1986, confirmed 2016)
standardsComparison.basis: WBGT + metabolic rate (kcal/h); standard man 70 kg, 1.8 m²
standardsComparison.structure: Continuous curves (4 work-rest lines: 15/30/45/60 min/h); no published discrete table
standardsComparison.notes: Current standard is NIOSH (2016), Pub. No. 2016-106, which confirmed 1986 curve values unchanged and removed 1986 ceiling limits. Recommended basis for HeatStressCalc.

standardsComparison.name: ACGIH TLV
standardsComparison.notes: Similar structure to NIOSH but different breakpoints; most used in industrial hygiene practice; not reproducible without license

standardsComparison.name: OSHA Heat Index (NIOSH joint)
standardsComparison.notes: Simpler, more accessible; does not differentiate by workload intensity; useful for field conditions without WBGT meter

standardsComparison.name: Cal/OSHA Title 8
standardsComparison.structure: Preventive cool-down rest ≥5 min; not scheduled cycling
standardsComparison.notes: Different regulatory model: mandatory "as needed" cooling rest, not fixed work-rest cycles; applies to outdoor and indoor workers

standardsComparison.name: EPA (1993) / NIOSH (2016) Table 6-2
standardsComparison.basis: Adjusted dry-bulb temp (°F) with RH and solar correction factors
standardsComparison.notes: Adapted from EPA (1993); reproduced in NIOSH (2016) as a practical field reference. Assumes physically fit, well-rested, fully hydrated, under age 40, 30% RH, natural ventilation. Different methodology from RAL/REL curves — uses ambient temp + adjustments, not WBGT.

intendedUse: This document is intended as a preliminary reference tool for occupational health education and policy development. It does not constitute a compliance standard or legal requirement. Users should verify intermediate work-rest line thresholds, apply professional judgment, and consult a certified industrial hygienist (CIH) for complex or high-hazard situations.
